title: The Longlight Kites
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fourth expansion pass
content:
The festival committee wanted Aang to teach everybody an Air Nomad sacred ceremony.

That was how the request reached us.

Pip had written a polite letter asking whether the Avatar might "share the beautiful flying traditions of his people" at the Longlight Kite Festival. They hadn't intended harm. The committee liked bright fabrics, impressive demonstrations, and the idea that one famous person could make a local celebration feel important.

Aang read the letter twice.

Then he set it down.

"That's not what kites are for," he said.

Toph leaned across the table.

"Usually they're for flying."

Katara hid a smile.

Aang looked at her.

"Don't encourage her."

"I'm not."

"You are."

I took the letter.

"What's wrong with the request?"

He rubbed the back of his neck.

"Some Air Nomad practices are meant to be taught in specific ways, by people who understand their meaning. I can show children how to make a kite. I can't turn every tradition I remember into entertainment for a festival."

The words were quiet, but there was grief beneath them.

The Longlight Festival belonged to Lanternweald, not to the Air Nomads. It had begun when the valley's stewards needed visible wind markers along the ridges before the winter storms. Families made bright cloth shapes and attached them to safe poles so travelers could see where the gusts were strongest. Over the years the wind markers became kites. Some people decorated them with symbols from home, but nobody had a claim on anyone else's sacred practices.

The committee had forgotten the difference between sharing a skill and borrowing a culture.

"Then we tell them," I said.

Aang nodded.

"I'll teach kite-making. But not a ceremony that isn't mine to give away."

We went to the meeting together.

Pip looked mortified when Aang explained.

"I didn't mean to make a spectacle of your people," they said.

"I know," Aang answered. "That's why I'm telling you."

The committee adjusted the program. The opening would explain the valley's own history of wind markers and safe travel routes. People could bring designs meaningful to them, but no one would be asked to display sacred symbols or explain private beliefs. Aang would teach balance, frame strength, and how to test a kite without endangering bystanders.

Tamsin approved the load limits. Fen marked the ridge where the wind was steady enough. Edda inspected the path to the viewing platform, and Danse offered to help secure the temporary railings.

Toph was suspicious.

"Are we doing another festival where the whole town thinks wood is indestructible?"

"Not this time," I said.

"Good. My patience has limits."

By the next morning the square was full of frames and colored cloth.

Aang sat on the floor with six children and two adults, teaching them how to tie a bridle knot. He was patient when the first kite twisted sideways. He didn't take it away and fix it. He asked which part felt uneven and let the child examine the string.

I thought of Lio's apprenticeship at Tideglass.

The lesson was spreading.

Katara helped a family choose lighter fabric because their child couldn't hold a heavy frame for long. Toph tested the stones beneath the launching area and declared one section too loose for running. We marked it off.

I made a kite with a pattern of small amber circles.

"Very original," Toph said.

"Thank you."

"It looks like a potato."

"That's cultural criticism, and I reject it."

She laughed.

Aang looked over.

"I like it."

"You would," Toph said. "You like anything that flies."

"That's not true."

She raised an eyebrow.

He considered.

"All right. Mostly true."

The first launch went badly.

My kite rose, tilted left, and fell into a patch of soft grass. The string tangled around my wrist.

Aang came toward me.

"Need help?"

"Yes. I need you to stop looking so pleased with yourself."

He grinned.

"That's not a repair."

"Can you help with the string?"

He sat beside me and showed me how to adjust the balance point. He didn't make the knot for me. It took three tries.

When the kite finally rose, the cloth caught the light. The amber circles shone against the sky.

I felt absurdly happy.

Aang watched it.

"That's beautiful," he said.

"It's a potato."

"A very graceful potato."

I laughed.

At the materials table, a boy named Lio arrived with a frame too heavy for the string he'd brought.

"I wanted it to be bigger than Maui's," he admitted.

Toph folded her arms.

"Then you wanted a kite or a monument?"

He looked offended.

"Both."

Katara knelt beside the frame and asked him to lift it as he would when the wind caught. He managed it for three seconds before his arms shook.

"Would you like to make a lighter version?" she asked.

Lio looked toward Maui, who had been asked to hold a line at the far end of the field.

"Will he laugh?"

"Absolutely," Toph said. "Then we'll laugh at his when it falls."

Aang sat with us and showed Lio how to trim the crossbar without weakening the center joint. He didn't take over the design. Lio chose a smaller sail, kept the original painted symbol, and wrote down the dimensions in his notebook so he could teach the next person.

When the kite finally lifted, Maui cheered so loudly that two others looked around.

Lio rolled his eyes. Then he grinned.

I thought about the apprentices at Brasswatch and the first boats at Tideglass. Skill was traveling between the districts without requiring everybody to become the same sort of person.

A volunteer came by to ask whether the event would run another hour. The sky was still bright, but Fen's wind board showed stronger gusts expected near dusk.

Aang checked the reading and shook his head.

"We close launches at the posted time. People can stay for food and music if they like."

He looked disappointed. He loved seeing the children fly, and I knew how much the afternoon meant to him.

"Are you okay?" I asked.

"Yes," he said, then corrected himself. "I'm sad to stop. That doesn't mean the rule is wrong."

Toph made a satisfied noise.

"Finally. An Avatar who understands weather isn't impressed by fame."

He stuck his tongue out at her.

I laughed, then helped roll the unused string for the next festival.

The festival continued through the afternoon. Some kites never flew. Some tore in the gusts. One child painted a fierce red bird that spun in circles before landing directly on Maui's head.

He declared it an act of war.

Nobody believed him.

Near sunset, Aang went to the edge of the ridge alone. I followed, leaving enough space for him to turn back if he wanted quiet.

"Mind company?" I asked.

He shook his head.

The sky was pale gold. Kites moved above the valley like small living shapes, each with a different line and angle. The old Threadway arches glowed below us, not as trophies but as paths people could choose.

"I miss them," Aang said.

I didn't need to ask who.

He looked at the kites.

"When people ask me to perform the traditions of the Air Nomads, part of me wants to say yes. I want them to know how beautiful my people were. I want the world to remember."

"And the other part?"

"Doesn't want their memory reduced to a show."

I took his hand.

"You get to decide what you share."

"Sometimes I feel selfish."

"Preserving meaning isn't selfish."

He looked at me.

"You sound like Katara."

"High compliment."

He smiled.

We stood together while the first evening lanterns came on.

"Can I ask you something?" he said.

"Of course."

"Do you ever feel pulled between everyone you love?"

"Yes."

"How do you know where you belong?"

I thought about the calendar at Riverstone, the quiet nights at Jasmine Steps, the workshop lights at Brasswatch, and the sea-glass orchard at Tideglass. I thought of Katara coming home, Toph choosing her own time, and Aang standing beside me with a history I could respect but never replace.

"I don't think belonging is a single place," I said. "I think it's the choices we keep making honestly."

He leaned close.

"That's a good answer."

"Don't let Toph hear you."

"She'll say it's a terrible answer."

"Then she'll steal it."

He laughed.

I kissed him under the first star, gentle and unhurried. The wind tugged at my hair and carried the sound of the festival up the ridge.

Later we packed away the kites that could be reused and labeled the damaged ones for repair. Aang helped without being asked to perform anything sacred.

At home, Katara had made tea. Toph was complaining about the potato kite.

I hung it by the window.

It looked ridiculous.

It was mine.
